analysis.one_liner: Forces nursing homes to test, report, and protect residents and workers during COVID, with paid sick leave and fines.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2021, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 public health emergency, nursing homes taking Medicare and Medicaid money would have had to test residents and staff for the virus, keep a full-time infection-prevention specialist on staff, give every employee at least two weeks of paid sick leave, and report cases, deaths, staffing, and protective-equipment supplies to the public every day. Facilities that broke the rules would owe $10,000 per day, and states would get $500 million to send rapid-response strike teams to outbreak facilities. It never moved beyond a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, and the low-wage aides and nurses who work in these facilities. Residents would get daily public reporting of cases, deaths, and staffing, protection from discharges and transfers not medically justified, and guaranteed visitation by phone or video. Workers would get paid sick leave, COVID testing before shifts, protective-equipment reporting, and enforcement of whistleblower protections during outbreaks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their low-wage aides

how_it_helps.text: Every Medicare and Medicaid nursing home would have to test residents weekly and employees before each shift, or screen for symptoms and daily report that it lacks test kits [S3].
Each facility must provide every employee at least two weeks of paid sick leave during the emergency period [S3].

Facilities must report cases, deaths, staffing levels, and protective-equipment supplies daily, and the government must publish that information within 24 hours on public websites families use to compare nursing homes [S3].
Operators would owe a civil penalty of $10,000 per day for each violation, including reporting false information [S3].

States would receive a share of $500 million to build strike teams — including National Guard members, public health officials, and resident and worker representatives — deployable within 72 hours of three or more diagnoses at a facility, to separate exposed people, supervise testing, and enforce whistleblower protections [S3].

Facilities could not discharge or transfer a resident without state approval, documented reasons, 72-hour notice, and the resident's written consent, and residents who stayed with family during the emergency could return for up to 180 days after it ended [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, who would bear the cost of testing, a full-time infection-prevention specialist, paid sick leave, daily public reporting, and up to $10,000 per day in fines for each violation. Taxpayers would fund the $500 million strike-team program through an authorized appropriation.

drawbacks.text: The requirements are real costs for facilities: a mandated full-time infection preventionist, weekly resident testing, pre-shift employee testing, and two weeks of paid sick leave for every employee, backed by $10,000-per-day penalties, would strain the budgets of nursing homes that operate on thin, largely government-funded margins [S3].

The rules applied only during the COVID-19 emergency period and to Medicare and Medicaid facilities; it left untouched the chronic understaffing and ownership-structure problems in the sector, and assisted living facilities would get only nonbinding guidance on virtual visitation and infection control [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of facilities where COVID killed tens of thousands, and for the workers who caught the virus on the job, the protections were substantial and targeted at the emergency's deadliest setting. The costs fall on operators, though some, like paid sick leave, would directly reduce the spread the bill is trying to stop. The bill's main design weakness is that it is emergency-only: once the emergency ended, the transparency and safety rules would lapse rather than become permanent standards.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 12, 2021, with Sen. Richard Blumenthal as its one cosponsor [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that was its final action [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators, who never had to absorb the testing, staffing, sick leave, or reporting requirements or the $10,000-per-day penalties. Residents and workers got nothing from the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators; residents and workers got nothing

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose testing, paid-sick-leave, transparency, and penalty requirements on Medicare and Medicaid nursing homes during the COVID emergency.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — never scheduled a markup or vote
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 12, 2021 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee never scheduled a markup or hearing on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. Both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but without a committee or floor action there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Nursing home operators (Medicare/Medicaid skilled nursing and nursing facilities)
industries.note: Operators would have absorbed testing, infection-prevention staffing, paid sick leave, daily public reporting of cases and deaths, and $10,000-per-day fines. Their interest in avoiding these requirements ran against residents' safety and workers' protections, which the record shows were the bill's entire purpose [S3].
Taxpayers would fund a $500 million strike-team program, in exchange for outbreak response in facilities whose care is largely publicly financed through Medicare and Medicaid [S3].
